words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as xiànzài. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 现在开始. Hindari: 现在 does not state duration — for “for ten minutes” you still need 十分钟.
words.when: Remember 现在 like the word you’ll use when you ask for a decision or give a status update right this moment — e.g. you’re free for a ten-minute work chat.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 现在 to pin the current moment in office talk (can we start, can we talk). Pair often with 现在开始. It marks “at this time,” not “for how long” — attach a duration phrase when you mean a span.

example.zh: 我现在有空，可以聊十分钟。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xiànzài yǒu kòng, kěyǐ liáo shí fēnzhōng.
example.en: I’m free now — we can talk for ten minutes.

words.en: in a bit; a little while
words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as yíhuìr. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 一会儿见. Hindari: do not use 一会儿 for an important deadline without a clear clock time.
words.when: Remember 一会儿 like the word you’ll use for a short, fuzzy pause in casual workplace talk — you’ll call back soon, not pinned to a minute.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 一会儿 for an imprecise short wait (一会儿见, 一会儿给你打电话). Fine for informal coordination; for work appointments that need certainty, give an actual time instead.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yíhuìr gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
example.en: I’ll call you in a bit.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as děng yíxià. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 等我一下. Hindari: 等一下 is not a promise that you’ll finish soon — give an estimate if the wait will be long.
words.when: Remember 等一下 like the word you’ll use when you need a pause before answering or acting at work — e.g. finish reading a message first.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers say 等一下 (or 等我一下) to buy a short beat before they reply or move. Add a reason when people have already been waiting. It stalls the conversation; it does not guarantee the task is almost done.

example.zh: 等一下，我先把这个消息看完。
example.pinyin: Děng yíxià, wǒ xiān bǎ zhège xiāoxi kàn wán.
example.en: Wait a moment — let me finish reading this message first.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as mǎshàng. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 马上回来. Hindari: do not say 马上 if you still have about an hour of other work left.
words.when: Remember 马上 like the word you’ll use when the action is already ready and will happen in a very short time — e.g. you’re heading to the meeting room now.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 马上 for something about to happen almost immediately (马上回来, 马上到). It implies readiness. Using it when you’re still buried in other work for an hour breaks trust.

example.en: I’ll be at the meeting room right away.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as xiān. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 先看一下. Hindari: 先 usually needs a following step or clear context.
words.when: Remember 先 like the word you’ll use when you mark the first step in a work sequence — confirm the time before you send the notice.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers put 先 before the first action in staged instructions (先看一下, 先确认时间). It expects a next step (often with 再) or a context that makes the sequence clear.

example.zh: 我们先确认时间，再发通知。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān quèrèn shíjiān, zài fā tōngzhī.
example.en: Let’s confirm the time first, then send the notice.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as zài. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 再决定. Hindari: 再 is for the next action; 又 is generally for a repetition that has already happened.
words.when: Remember 再 like the word you’ll use when you link the next workplace step after the first one is done — look at the file, then discuss.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 再 for the subsequent action in a process (先……再……, 再决定). Do not swap in 又 for that “then” sense — 又 usually marks something that already happened again.

example.zh: 你先看文件，我们再讨论。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiān kàn wénjiàn, wǒmen zài tǎolùn.
example.en: You look at the document first, then we’ll discuss.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as zhīqián. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 下班之前. Hindari: do not confuse with 以前, which often points to a more general past period.
words.when: Remember 之前 like the word you’ll use when you set a deadline before an event or clock — reply before end of workday.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers attach 之前 after a time noun or event (下班之前, 会议之前) to mean “before that point.” 以前 is broader “in the past / formerly,” not the same tight before-deadline sense.

example.pinyin: Qǐng zài xiàbān zhīqián huífù wǒ.
example.en: Please reply to me before you leave work.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as zhīhòu. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 会议之后. Hindari: after a verb, use patterns like 开会之后; do not drop the event context.
words.when: Remember 之后 like the word you’ll use when the next work step comes after a point in time or an event — after the meeting, lock the next step.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers put 之后 after a noun or verb phrase naming the event (会议之后, 开会之后). Keep the event clear; bare 之后 without that anchor is hard to follow in workplace talk.

example.zh: 会议之后，我们再确定下一步。
example.pinyin: Huìyì zhīhòu, wǒmen zài quèdìng xià yí bù.
example.en: After the meeting, we’ll confirm the next step.

words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as tíqián. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 提前通知. Hindari: 提前 is not merely “faster” while moving; it means earlier than the schedule.
words.when: Remember 提前 like the word you’ll use when a schedule moves up or you need notice before a deadline — tell me early if the time changes.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 提前 for doing or saying something earlier than planned (提前通知, 提前告诉我). It is about beating the schedule, not moving physically faster.

example.zh: 如果时间有变化，请提前告诉我。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ shíjiān yǒu biànhuà, qǐng tíqián gàosu wǒ.
example.en: If the time changes, please tell me in advance.

words.en: on schedule; according to the timetable
words.note: Book headword pinyin printed as ànshí. Example-sentence pinyin not printed in the book; standard pinyin added. Pairing in book: 按时完成. Hindari: 按时 and 准时 are similar; 准时 stresses hitting an exact time point, 按时 stresses following the schedule.
words.when: Remember 按时 like the word you’ll use when people must show up or deliver according to the set schedule — attend the meeting as planned.
words.usage: Most Chinese speakers use 按时 for compliance with a timetable (按时参加, 按时完成). Prefer 准时 when you mean punctuality at a exact clock moment; use 按时 when the point is sticking to the planned schedule.

example.en: Please everyone attend the meeting on schedule.

notes.title: Module aim — time without ambiguity
notes.body: Modul 02 / Harian (book pages 9–11): talk about sequence, short waits, and deadlines without letting people misread your timing. Indonesian title in the book: Waktu dan janji. No multi-speaker dialogue or passage is printed in this module (simulations start later in the book).

notes.title: 现在 / 一会儿 / 等一下 / 马上 — how soon?
notes.body: From the book’s Hindari notes: 现在 marks the current moment, not a duration (still say 十分钟 for “for ten minutes”). 一会儿 is a short fuzzy wait — fine casually, but give a clock time for important work deadlines. 等一下 buys a pause before you answer or act; it is not a promise you will finish soon — estimate if the wait will be long. 马上 means the action is ready and almost immediate; do not say it if you still have about an hour of other work.

example.en: I’ll be at the meeting room right away.

notes.title: 先……再…… for staged work steps
notes.body: 先 marks the first step in a sequence and usually needs a following step or clear context (pairing: 先看一下). 再 links the next action after that first step (pairing: 再决定). The book contrasts 再 (next action) with 又 (generally a repetition that already happened).

example.zh: 我们先确认时间，再发通知。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān quèrèn shíjiān, zài fā tōngzhī.
example.en: Let’s confirm the time first, then send the notice.

notes.title: 之前 vs 以前; 之后 needs an event
notes.body: 之前 attaches after a time noun or event as a before-deadline boundary (下班之前). Do not swap in 以前, which often means a more general past. 之后 means after a point or event (会议之后); after a verb, keep patterns like 开会之后 and do not drop the event context.

example.pinyin: Qǐng zài xiàbān zhīqián huífù wǒ.
example.en: Please reply to me before you leave work.

notes.title: 提前 vs 按时 (and 准时)
notes.body: 提前 means earlier than the schedule (提前通知) — not merely “moving faster.” 按时 stresses sticking to the timetable (按时完成 / 按时参加). 准时 is close but highlights hitting an exact time point; 按时 highlights following the schedule.

example.zh: 如果时间有变化，请提前告诉我。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ shíjiān yǒu biànhuà, qǐng tíqián gàosu wǒ.
example.en: If the time changes, please tell me in advance.

notes.title: Latihan 90 detik (book exercise)
notes.body: Book drill on p.11: pick three entries from this module — 现在, 先, and 提前 — and build one work or daily story that uses all three. Record without reading the PDF, then check whether your timing and decisions came out clearly. No model Chinese dialogue is printed for this drill; do not invent one as book text.

example.en: Target trio for the 90-second practice (instruction only; no sample story in the book).
